newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: INTERVIEW - Bangladesh moves to end banking crisis.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Bangladesh moves to end banking crisis.

text.p: Bangladesh said on Saturday it was taking all necessary measures, including a tightening of existing legal provisions and improvement of management, to deal with a crisis facing its banking sector caused by the large volume of bad loans.
Finance ministry officials said a high-level government meeting attended by Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria and Law Minister Abdul Matin Khasru was held on Saturday to discuss the sector's problems.
"Thousands of cases relating to bank loans are outstanding with the country's loan courts," Syed Amirul Mulk, secretary of the finance ministry's Banking Division, told Reuters in an interview.
"Steps are being taken to see the courts are engaged exclusively for trying cases relating to bank loans," he said.
The government moves followed a statement by Bangladesh Bank (central bank) governor Lutfar Rahman Sarkar that the country's banking system was on the verge of collapse.

Sarkar said on Tuesday that the country's commercial banks had a burden of 130 billion taka ($3 billion) in bad loans, and warned that Bangladesh law was not adequate to deal with the loan defaulters.
Central bank officials said on Friday that the government had decided to provide commercial banks with some 16 billion taka ($368 million) to tide them over their liquidity problems.

Mulk said procedures for settling the loan cases had been complicated, which had delayed legal verdicts. "(But) a recent amendment to the loan court act has now made it possible to make execution of suits simultaneously."
"We are now trying to find out whether the existing laws can be made more stringent. We have already enacted a bankruptcy act and I hope this will help recovery of the loans," he said.
Mulk said the government was also taking up a project, financed by Japan, to reform the commercial banking system with the help of the World Bank.
"A team of World Bank consultants will come here soon to look into (the banking system) and advise the government on commercial banking reforms," he said.
"The team would suggest modernisation and rationalisation of the banks. The work of the team will start in May."
Mulk said it was long-term loans that had created the problem in the banking sector. "The classified loans should be reduced as quickly as possible," he said.
He said a substantial portion of the classified loans was due from public sector enterprises. "If banks can collect these loans their liquidity position will improve," he added.
